scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: Capitalism should eventually be superseded by a socialised economy, even if the road there is gradual.
Reforms are worthwhile mainly insofar as they build toward eventually replacing capitalism.
A fully socialised economy remains the ultimate goal, whatever compromises the present requires.
Private ownership of the major means of production is a problem to be solved, not managed indefinitely.
The welfare state is a stage on the way to something beyond capitalism, not the final destination.
Socialists should keep the horizon of a post-capitalist economy alive, even while working within the current one.
A well-regulated capitalism with a strong welfare state is not a stage toward something else; it is the goal.
Taming capitalism's worst effects is a full and sufficient program, not a first step toward abolishing it.
There is no need to imagine an economy beyond capitalism as long as capitalism can be made humane enough.
Permanent management of capitalism through democratic institutions is preferable to any attempt to replace it.
A regulated market economy, indefinitely sustained, is compatible with a genuinely socialist commitment.
The point of socialism is to civilise capitalism, not to end it.
Key industries should be brought into state or public ownership.
Nationalisation of major utilities and infrastructure is a legitimate and often necessary policy.
The state is the right vehicle to own and run large-scale enterprise on behalf of the public.
Public ownership, properly managed, outperforms private ownership in essential sectors.
A government elected to represent the public should be willing to take strategic industries into public hands.
State ownership removes profit-seeking from decisions that affect everyone.
Worker and consumer cooperatives are a better model of social ownership than a state-run enterprise.
Ownership should be devolved to workers' and users' associations rather than centralised in the state.
A cooperative economy avoids the bureaucratic distance that state ownership creates between the enterprise and the people it serves.
Mutual and cooperative ownership better reflects democratic control than a ministry ever could.
The state is too remote from day-to-day production to be the right owner of most enterprise.
Associational forms of ownership, not nationalisation, are the socialist alternative to private capital.
Organised labour, through unions and mass parties, is the driving force of social progress.
Real gains for working people have historically come from mobilised labour movements, not from enlightened administration alone.
A socialist party without a rooted labour movement behind it has no real base.
Strikes and organised labour pressure remain a legitimate and necessary part of achieving social democratic goals.
The trade union movement should have a formal, structural role inside a social democratic party.
Mass membership and mobilisation are what give a labour party its legitimacy and power.
Competent technocratic administration and expert policy design deliver more reliable progress than mass mobilisation does.
A well-run civil service can achieve more for ordinary people than industrial action ever could.
Modern social democracy is better served by expert governance than by dependence on trade union power.
Professional policymaking, insulated from union pressure, produces more sustainable reform.
The labour movement's role should be advisory rather than decisive in shaping government policy.
Sound administration matters more to social democracy's success than the strength of any particular movement behind it.
Society is organised around a real conflict between labour and capital, and social democracy exists to represent labour's side of it.
Political parties should be honest that they represent the interests of a particular class, not the nation as a whole.
The interests of workers and the interests of employers are, at bottom, opposed.
A social democratic party should see itself as the political expression of the labour movement.
Redistribution is justified because capital's gains come at labour's expense.
Class remains the primary division that social democratic politics has to organise around.
The national interest, properly understood, unites workers and employers more than it divides them.
Government should represent the whole nation, not act as the political arm of any one class.
Cross-class cooperation between labour and capital is possible and preferable to permanent conflict.
Framing politics as a struggle between classes is a distortion that a modern social democracy should move past.
Employers and employees share a common interest in a growing, well-managed economy.
Class-based politics narrows a party's appeal in ways that hurt rather than help ordinary people.
Socialism's case rests on ethical conviction and human solidarity as much as on any theory of economic development.
A religious or humanist sense of duty toward the poor is a legitimate foundation for socialist commitment.
Fellowship and mutual obligation are the moral core of the socialist project, not just its material programme.
Socialism should be defended as a moral vision of how people ought to treat one another, not only as economic analysis.
The case for social democracy can rest on conscience and compassion without needing a theory of historical stages.
Ethical conviction is a sufficient basis for socialist politics on its own.
Socialist policy should be grounded in a materialist analysis of economic development, not in moral sentiment.
Appeals to ethics and conscience are a weaker foundation for politics than an analysis of class interest.
The case for redistribution should rest on structural economic argument, not on charity or compassion.
Socialism is a scientific analysis of capitalism's development, not primarily a moral creed.
Grounding policy in sentiment rather than economic analysis makes for worse, less durable politics.
A social democratic programme should be justified by its material outcomes, not by an appeal to conscience.
Markets, properly regulated and taxed, are a reasonably efficient way to allocate most goods.
A mixed economy with strong regulation and a robust welfare state is preferable to comprehensive planning.
Private enterprise, operating within rules set democratically, can be compatible with a socialist programme.
Central planning across the whole economy is neither necessary nor desirable to achieve social democratic goals.
Markets can be harnessed for social ends through taxation and regulation rather than replaced outright.
A competitive market sector, combined with strong public services, is the practical model worth pursuing.
The economy as a whole should be organised through comprehensive democratic planning, not left to market allocation.
Relying on markets, even regulated ones, leaves too much power in private hands to be a real socialist model.
Planning, not market incentives, should determine what gets produced and how it's distributed.
A market economy, however regulated, still runs on the logic of profit, which planning would remove.
Serious social democrats should aim to replace market allocation with democratic planning over time.
Trusting markets to deliver socially desirable outcomes, even with regulation, concedes too much to capital.
Solidarity between workers of different countries should take priority over any one nation's programme.
International labour and socialist organisation matters as much as winning power in any single country.
A social democratic government should coordinate with sister parties abroad rather than act purely in national terms.
The labour movement's outlook should be internationalist even when its immediate battles are fought at home.
Building international institutions of solidarity is a legitimate priority for a socialist movement.
Workers everywhere share more in common with each other than with the capital of their own country.
A social democratic party's first obligation is to the workers of its own nation.
National programmes, tailored to national conditions, should take priority over international coordination.
Practical social democracy is built one country at a time, not through international schemes.
The nation remains the primary framework within which social democratic gains are actually won and defended.
International solidarity is a worthy sentiment but a secondary concern next to winning power at home.
A social democratic government answers to its own electorate first, international solidarity second.
Winning elections and governing through parliament is the legitimate route to social democratic change.
Working through existing constitutional and parliamentary institutions is both practical and principled.
A social democratic party should aim to win office and legislate its programme through the state.
Reform through the ballot box has delivered real, lasting gains for working people.
Patient parliamentary work, however slow, is more durable than any shortcut around it.
The state, once captured through elections, is a legitimate and sufficient instrument for social democratic change.
Lasting change requires building movement institutions — unions, cooperatives, mutual societies — that operate alongside and sometimes against the state.
Relying solely on parliament leaves a movement vulnerable whenever it loses an election.
Parallel structures of working-class power should be built regardless of who holds government office.
A movement's own institutions, not just its parliamentary representatives, are what secure real, lasting gains.
Electoral office is only one part of building power; movement infrastructure outside the state matters as much.
Depending only on the state for change cedes too much of the movement's independence.
